title: Error Handling Strategy
subtopics: Mapping domain errors to HTTP responses
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of error handling strategy in a FastAPI application.
Apply or interpret one example related to client errors versus server errors.
Identify one limitation or failure case and describe how to verify it.

content.intro: This lesson covers error handling strategy within responses, errors, and validation. Use the supplied syllabus topics as the coverage checklist, then connect them to the worked example and the verification task.
content.why_it_matters: You will use error handling strategy to build APIs whose contracts and behavior are understandable to both clients and maintainers. The practical aim is repeatable checks, explicit expected outcomes, negative cases and actionable diagnostics.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Error Handling Strategy matters because it is part of responses, errors, and validation. In practice, focus on repeatable checks, explicit expected outcomes, negative cases and actionable diagnostics. A framework feature only helps when its assumptions match the application; keep input validation, business policy and side effects distinguishable.

items.title: Client errors versus server errors
items.text: Use client errors versus server errors to make behavior observable and repeatable. Specify one normal case, one invalid or missing-input case, and the expected status or diagnostic. A passing happy path alone is not enough evidence.

content_blocks.reset_steps: For read-only examples, no reset is needed. For any example that writes state, use a disposable local database/test fixture; record the starting state and clean up only lab data. Never use production credentials or real personal data.

Run it only in a local virtual environment or a separately isolated runner with resource/time/network limits. content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Adapt the example to cover “Client errors versus server errors”. Write down the expected success result and one invalid, missing, duplicate, timeout or permission-boundary case that matters for this topic.

task: Create a small reviewable artifact for “Error Handling Strategy”: explain its goal, cover the listed subtopics, show an example with expected result, then include one edge case and how you would verify it.
hints: Start with “Client errors versus server errors” and state the required inputs, output and assumptions.
Change one thing at a time; check the official reference and capture the actual response/error instead of guessing.
Include a negative/edge-case check and document which behavior remains untested.
expected_output: A reviewable example or design note for Error Handling Strategy, covering the PDF subtopics, expected behavior and at least one verification check.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a code fragment without checking its assumptions.
common_mistakes.why: Installed versions, imported types, application structure and external services affect behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: State assumptions; check the versioned official docs; run a minimal local test and add one failure case.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating one happy-path response as proof of correctness.
common_mistakes.why: Invalid input, permissions, concurrency, timeouts and cleanup are not exercised by a single request.
common_mistakes.fix: Add focused normal and negative tests and record exact expected status/body.

common_mistakes.why: Even short examples may mutate records, reveal data or affect availability.
common_mistakes.fix: Use synthetic inputs and a disposable environment; review security, cleanup and rollback before promotion.

summary: Error Handling Strategy belongs to the broader goal of repeatable checks, explicit expected outcomes, negative cases and actionable diagnostics.
Use the source subtopics as the completeness checklist and verify expected results rather than relying on intuition.
Examples in this course are illustrative until technically reviewed and executed on a supported local environment.
